question: The Commission has adopted a strategy for developing and deploying small modular reactors, which recognises the role that they can play across the wider energy system, not only in generating electricity but also in providing heat. In the current geopolitical context – especially considering Russia’s war of aggression – strengthening Europe’s energy self-sufficiency is a necessity.

In this regard, small modular reactors offer a way of increasing stable energy production while reducing the EU’s dependence on external energy sources. Nuclear energy is also clean. However, many of the proposed EU-level actions on this important technology remain quite general.

Europe’s energy system would benefit from more concrete actions that would help ensure that these crucial objectives – reducing the EU’s energy dependency and increasing stable production – are actually achieved. In this context: 1.
Will the Commission ensure that the upcoming proposals for the post-2030 energy and climate framework are fully in line with the objectives of this strategy?

What additional financial instruments does the Commission plan to introduce post-2028 to support first-of-a-kind nuclear projects and the scaling-up of commercially viable innovative nuclear technologies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) The Commission’s work towards a more flexible, investment-driven and delivery-focused Energy Union1 in post-2030 build on the actions taken under the Affordable Energy Action Plan, which include the Small Modular Reactors Strategy adopted on 10 March 20262, and the recently adopted AccelerateEU Communication3 and Electrification Action Plan4.

For those Member States choosing nuclear energy, the Commission has recognised that nuclear can contribute to decarbonisation, competitiveness, security of supply and strategic autonomy5. In that context, the Commission will continue to uphold the principle of technology neutrality across all policy and legislative initiatives, while fully respecting Member States’ right to determine their energy mix6.

The Commission proposal for the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) to apply from 2028 onwards is currently being negotiated with the budgetary authority. The Commission respects the process and does not wish to speculate on its outcomes.

In parallel, the Commission works with the European Investment Bank to implement, already in the current MFF, a temporary InvestEU top up of EUR 200 million until 20287 to support innovative nuclear technologies8.

Other relevant avenues to fund nuclear investments in the EU already pursued include the prospective Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEI) on innovative nuclear technologies9 and the Scaleup Europe Fund10 as well as funding for nuclear research and innovation activities under the Euratom Research and Training Programme.
